⟨\text{_______}\,,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [0,\pi ]$ is given above. What is the $1$st component of the product?" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\ge 0$ for all $x\in [0,\pi ].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(x,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ and

$$
D={(x,\theta )\,:\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂x},\,\frac{∂y}{∂x},\,\frac{∂z}{∂x}⟩=⟨1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨0,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′},\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-247cda82-3b8b-57b4-bd85-1eaf3e646212"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id r(z,\theta )=⟨\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\text{__________},\,z⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $r(z,\theta )$ above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x=\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}$ by  $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis for $z\in [1,5].$ What is the second  component of $r?$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/d3/d3302b5f4ea4c0387d70ac8f78e03e486fff9579f1a6b5e5cec08a31cde76af3.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $x=f(z)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,z\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $x=f(z)=\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}\ge 0$ for all $z\in [1,5].$   

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
r(z,\theta )=⟨\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,z\in [1,5],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Therefore, the second component of $r$ is $\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields What is the $3$rd component of the product?" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $y=\sqrt{z-1}\ge 0$ for all $z\in [1,10].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is  

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,(z,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(z)=\sqrt{z-1},$ and  

$$
D={(z,\theta )\,:\,1\le z\le 10,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=\sqrt{z-1},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z-1}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨\sqrt{z-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\sqrt{z-1}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f2a4e677-4714-5cf2-98da-8e4b0964eb3f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id [-\pi ,\pi ].$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{2})\ge 0$ for all $y\in [-\pi ,\pi ].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{2}),$ and

$$
D={(y,\theta )\,:\,-\pi \le y\le \pi ,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y}\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′},\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f{f}^{′})^{2}+(f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{2}),$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(y)=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2}).$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{2})\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2}))}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{2})\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{y}{2})}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-47b1c789-64a3-55f5-9e7d-ac42dc183f0e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′},\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y}\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f{f}^{′})^{2}+(f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $x=f(z)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,z\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $x=f(z)=\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}\ge 0$ for all $z\in [1,5].$   

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
r(z,\theta )=⟨\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,z\in [1,5],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Therefore, the second component of $r$ is $\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$"] ["question-a20cac79-e438-5720-941d-255bfdc76ec3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] $$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{2}),$ and

$$
D={(y,\theta )\,:\,-\pi \le y\le \pi ,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y}\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′},\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f{f}^{′})^{2}+(f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$"] ["question-b858f50b-1a14-576c-973e-c7199e8e8cdb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-47b1c789-64a3-55f5-9e7d-ac42dc183f0e" :answer-field/id #uuid $z\in [-1,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,(z,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(z)=1+{z}^{4},$ and

$$
D={(z,\theta )\,:\,-1\le z\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+({f}^{′}f)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(z)=1+{z}^{4},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(z)=4{z}^{3}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(1+{z}^{4})\sqrt{1+(4{z}^{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(1+{z}^{4})\sqrt{1+16{z}^{6}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186371948 :question/id #uuid "1297d2b2-529f-5b54-8024-028cb62e9052" :question/math-academy-id "q-161098"} {:db/id 17592186389126 :question/id #uuid 17592186172933 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173175 :tutorial/content "Consider the planar curve $y=e^{-x}$ defined on the interval $x \in [0,2],$ as shown below.

![](images/a8/a8ce2449af085548fecc543fbd5ccfec0e8024344547b2a7825f3a6e9ccf63d4.png)

By rotating this curve $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we get a **surface of revolution**:

![](images/88/88c9c1ec629ab9967cc011aaadafebea255cd50abee9c3730bed4f53f671c71b.png)

We can parametrize this surface in the following way:

- We take a point $P$ on the surface with $x$-coordinate equal to $x_0$ for some fixed $x_0 \in [0,2].$

- Now, by taking the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=x_0,$ we get a circle of radius $e^{-x_0}.$

![](images/f1/f1e2cf1c571a21e06f1b25f99a64b5529fea8c65c897b3f225cfd0d307d725d7.png)

 
This circle can be parameterized as follows:

$$
\mathbf r(x_0, \theta) = \big\langle {\color{black}x_0}, \: e^{-x_0} \, \cos{\theta}, \: e^{-x_0} \, \sin{\theta} \big\rangle,
\quad  \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

- Finally, by allowing $x_0$ to vary over the interval $[0, 2],$ these circles will trace out the surface of revolution. Therefore, our parameterization is

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = \big\langle x, \: e^{-x} \cos{\theta}, \: e^{-x}\sin{\theta} \big\rangle,
\quad 
x \in [0,2], 
\quad
\theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

Let's now describe some general formulas for parametrizing surfaces of revolution." :tutorial/id #uuid "9bd13796-1bf7-5a1b-a9f4-87567fd6998c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5305 :tutorial/title :tutorial/content "Consider the point $(x(y),y,0)$ that lies on the curve $x=x(y)\geq 0$ for $y\in [a,b]$ in the $xy$-plane. Rotating this point by $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis generates a circle, as shown below.

![](images/98/981ed341198c54e5dffeae770d13b3d46222ad429d0315ecd057b43995b4c0d6.png)

The pair $(\textrm{circle}_1,\textrm{circle}_2)$ denotes any parametrization of a circle of radius $x(y)$ with parameter $y.$

Using arguments similar to those seen earlier, the corresponding surface of revolution can be parametrized as

$$
\mathbf{r} = \big\langle x(y) \cos\theta, \: y, \: x(y) \sin\theta \big\rangle, \quad y\in[a,b], \quad \theta\in [0,2\pi).
$$

**Note:** Since a parametrization of a circle is not unique, we can obtain different parameterizations of our surface of revolution. For example, the following is also a valid parameterization:
\[ 
\mathbf{r} = \big\langle x(y) \sin\theta, \: y, \: x(y) \cos\theta \big\rangle, \quad y\in[a,b], \quad \theta\in [0,2\pi). 
\]

Similarly, the rotation of a point $(0,y,z(y))$ on the curve $z=z(y)\geq 0$ in the $yz$-plane about the $y$-axis can be visualized as follows:

![](images/59/5936d54e55c151ec2d9786a3ce2bd807970a71c10a21974562fd601bf50dfd37.png)

The corresponding surface of revolution can be parametrized as

$$
\mathbf{r} = \big\langle z(y) \cos\theta, \: y, \: z(y) \sin\theta \big\rangle, \quad y\in[a,b], \quad \theta\in [0,2\pi).
$$

As mentioned previously, neither of these parameterizations is unique.

**Note:** Since a parametrization of a circle is not unique, we can obtain different parameterizations of our surface of revolution. For example, the following is also a valid parameterization:
\[
\mathbf{r} = \big\langle z(y) \sin\theta, \: y, \: z(y) \cos\theta \big\rangle, \quad y\in[a,b], \quad \theta\in [0,2\pi). 
\]" :tutorial/id #uuid "ae882ec8-1ebd-5277-8224-b440b433c8ee" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5507 :tutorial/title "Formulas for Rotation About the y-Axis"} :step/id #uuid "23271cc4-5b18-5ab7-87a0-420c4bf3d6fc" :step/math-academy-id 34312 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173087}} {:db/id 17592186173083 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172132 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171712 :question/id #uuid "8ed57b1f-0082-5281-b061-ff2020ed7d66" :question/math-academy-id "e-12364"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4df896f9-7094-5d49-a5cf-3d0f62164298" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048384}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172233} {:db/id 17592186172379} {:db/id 17592186278362} {:db/id 17592186278367} {:db/id 17592186278368} {:db/id 17592186278372} {:db/id 17592186278373} {:db/id 17592186401212}] :knowledge-point/title "The Fundamental Vector Product of a Surface of Revolution"} :step/id #uuid "2109942c-c8ff-56d5-8311-ec29a24f7390" :step/math-academy-id 44310 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173084}} {:db/id 17592186173084 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173253 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $S$ is a surface parametrized by a differentiable vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle x(u,v), \: y(u,v), \: z(u,v) \big\rangle
$$

defined over a region $D$ in the $uv$-plane, then the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \: \textrm{d}S =  \iint\limits_{D} \| \mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v  \| \: \textrm{d}A,
$$

where $\mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v$ is the fundamental vector product of the surface.

Let's apply this formula to find the surface area generated by a surface of revolution.

Suppose that the curve [math]y=f(x)[/math] for [math]x \in [a,b][/math] is rotated [math]2\pi[/math] radians about the [math]x[/math]-axis. The corresponding surface of revolution can be parametrized as

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{r} = \big\langle x, \: f(x) \cos\theta, \: f(x) \sin\theta \big\rangle, \quad (x,\theta) \in D, 
\end{align*}

where [math]D= \big\{ (x,\theta) \: : \: x \in[a,b], \: \theta \in [0,2\pi) \big\}.[/math] How can we find the area of this surface?

First, we now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{r}'_x 
&= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial x}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial x}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} \bigg\rangle 
= \big\langle 1, \:f'(x) \cos\theta, \: f'(x) \sin\theta \big\rangle \\[10pt]

\mathbf{r}'_\theta 
&= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial \theta} \bigg\rangle 
= \big\langle 0, \: -f(x) \sin\theta, \: f(x) \cos\theta \big\rangle
\end{align*}

Next, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta 
&= 
\begin{vmatrix}
\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\
1 & f'(x) \cos\theta & f'(x) \sin\theta \\
0 & -f(x) \sin\theta & f(x) \cos\theta
\end{vmatrix} \\[5pt]
&= \bigg\langle \begin{vmatrix} f'(x) \cos\theta & f'(x) \sin\theta \\ -f(x) \sin\theta & f(x) \cos\theta \end{vmatrix}, \: -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & f'(x) \sin\theta \\ 0  & f(x) \cos\theta \end{vmatrix}, \: \begin{vmatrix} 1 & f'(x) \cos\theta \\ 0 & -f(x) \sin\theta  \end{vmatrix} \bigg\rangle \\[5pt]
&= \big\langle f(x)f'(x)\cos^2\theta+f(x)f'(x)\sin^2\theta, \: -f(x) \cos\theta, \: -f(x)\sin\theta \big\rangle \\[5pt]
&= \big\langle f(x)f'(x), \: -f(x) \cos\theta, \:- f(x)\sin\theta \big\rangle
\end{align*}

and

\begin{align*}
\left\|  \mathbf{r}'_y \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta \right\|
&= \sqrt{\big( f(x)f'(x) \big)^2 + \big( -f(x) \cos\theta \big)^2 + \big( -f(x)\sin\theta \big)^2 } \\[3pt]
&= \sqrt{\big(f(x)\big)^2\big(f'(x)\big)^2 + \big(f(x)\big)^2 \big( \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta \big) } \\[3pt]
&= \sqrt{\big(f(x)\big)^2\big(f'(x)\big)^2 + \big(f(x)\big)^2 } \\[3pt]
&= f(x) \sqrt{1 + \big(f'(x)\big)^2 }.
\end{align*}

Therefore, the surface area is

\begin{align*}
A 
&= \iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S \\[5pt]
&= \iint\limits_D  \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_y \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta \right\|  \text{d}x\text{d}\theta \\[5pt]
&= \int_{a}^{b} \int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x) \sqrt{1 + \big(f'(x)\big)^2 } \: \text{d}\theta \: \text{d}x \\[5pt]
&= \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \sqrt{1 + \big(f'(x)\big)^2} \: \text{d}x \cdot \int_{0}^{2\pi}  \text{d}\theta \\[5pt]
&= \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \sqrt{1 + \big(f'(x)\big)^2} \: \text{d}x \cdot \big[ \theta \big]_{0}^{2\pi}  \\[5pt]
&= 2\pi \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\sqrt{1 + \big(f'(x)\big)^2 } \: \text{d}x.
\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "79f42de8-4cc4-576a-b367-c08bd87f8bcd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7638 :tutorial/title "Computing a Surface Area of Revolution"} :step/id #uuid "8c37f4ed-7df7-5a6c-855e-263d81b3f5b0" :step/math-academy-id 44313 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173085}} {:db/id 17592186173085 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172133 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171713 :question/id #uuid "a2ff0c76-0d26-51a2-a2fb-498ff5f85559" :question/math-academy-id "e-12365"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4d7d1683-4735-5c93-9ad1-542e987aed1d" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172232} {:db/id 17592186172380} {:db/id 17592186278375} {:db/id 17592186278376} {:db/id 17592186278377} {:db/id 17592186278378} {:db/id 17592186371941} {:db/id 17592186371948} {:db/id 17592186389126}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Surface of Revolution"} :step/id #uuid "3533d6b6-1b8e-5af8-b6c0-195bca89c86d" :step/math-academy-id 44314} {:db/id 17592186173086 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173254 :tutorial/content "Consider the point $(x,y(x),0)$ that lies on the curve $y=y(x)$ in the $xy$-plane. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3148fb53-9ae7-5747-aa63-b79dd1bc224f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7648 :tutorial/title "Parametrizing a Surface Generated by Rotating y=y(x) About the x-Axis"} :step/id #uuid "93cfa70b-b133-5659-9bce-ab370759c49e" :step/math-academy-id 44408 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173089}} {:db/id 17592186173087 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173255 :tutorial/content "Now consider the point $(x(z),0,z)$ on the curve $x=x(z)\geq 0$ for $z\in [a,b]$ in the $xz$-plane. Rotating this point by $2\pi$ radians about the $z$-axis generates a circle, as shown below.

Finally, the rotation of a point $(0,y(z),z)$ on a curve $y=y(z)\geq 0$ in the $yz$-plane about the $z$-axis can be visualized as follows:

![](images/5f/5ff1574db4d105e7d69cc12ed609898d626b4977902f98dbcbcac6633ad56d2b.png)

The corresponding surface of revolution can be parametrized as

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle x(u,v), \: y(u,v), \: z(u,v) \big\rangle
$$

defined over a region $D$ in the $uv$-plane, then the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \: \textrm{d}S =  \iint\limits_{D} \| \mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v  \| \: \textrm{d}A,
$$

where $\mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v$ is the fundamental vector product of the surface.

Let's apply this formula to find the surface area generated by a surface of revolution.

Suppose that the curve [math]y=f(x)[/math] for [math]x \in [a,b][/math] is rotated [math]2\pi[/math] radians about the [math]x[/math]-axis. The corresponding surface of revolution can be parametrized as

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{r} = \big\langle x, \: f(x) \cos\theta, \: f(x) \sin\theta \big\rangle, \quad (x,\theta) \in D, 
\end{align*}

where [math]D= \big\{ (x,\theta) \: : \: x \in[a,b], \: \theta \in [0,2\pi) \big\}.[/math] How can we find the area of this surface?

First, we now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{r}'_x 
&= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial x}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial x}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} \bigg\rangle 
= \big\langle 1, \:f'(x) \cos\theta, \: f'(x) \sin\theta \big\rangle \\[10pt]

\mathbf{r}'_\theta 
&= \bigg\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial \theta} \bigg\rangle 
= \big\langle 0, \: -f(x) \sin\theta, \: f(x) \cos\theta \big\rangle
\end{align*}

Next, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta 
&= 
\begin{vmatrix}
\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\
1 & f'(x) \cos\theta & f'(x) \sin\theta \\
0 & -f(x) \sin\theta & f(x) \cos\theta
\end{vmatrix} \\[5pt]
&= \bigg\langle \begin{vmatrix} f'(x) \cos\theta & f'(x) \sin\theta \\ -f(x) \sin\theta & f(x) \cos\theta \end{vmatrix}, \: -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & f'(x) \sin\theta \\ 0  & f(x) \cos\theta \end{vmatrix}, \: \begin{vmatrix} 1 & f'(x) \cos\theta \\ 0 & -f(x) \sin\theta  \end{vmatrix} \bigg\rangle \\[5pt]
&= \big\langle f(x)f'(x)\cos^2\theta+f(x)f'(x)\sin^2\theta, \: -f(x) \cos\theta, \: -f(x)\sin\theta \big\rangle \\[5pt]
&= \big\langle f(x)f'(x), \: -f(x) \cos\theta, \:- f(x)\sin\theta \big\rangle
\end{align*}

and

\begin{align*}
\left\|  \mathbf{r}'_y \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta \right\|
&= \sqrt{\big( f(x)f'(x) \big)^2 + \big( -f(x) \cos\theta \big)^2 + \big( -f(x)\sin\theta \big)^2 } \\[3pt]
&= \sqrt{\big(f(x)\big)^2\big(f'(x)\big)^2 + \big(f(x)\big)^2 \big( \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta \big) } \\[3pt]
&= \sqrt{\big(f(x)\big)^2\big(f'(x)\big)^2 + \big(f(x)\big)^2 } \\[3pt]
&= f(x) \sqrt{1 + \big(f'(x)\big)^2 }.
\end{align*}

Therefore, the surface area is

\begin{align*}
A 
&= \iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S \\[5pt]
&= \iint\limits_D  \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_y \times \mathbf{r}'_\theta \right\|  \text{d}x\text{d}\theta \\[5pt]
&= \int_{a}^{b} \int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x) \sqrt{1 + \big(f'(x)\big)^2 } \: \text{d}\theta \: \text{d}x \\[5pt]
&= \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \sqrt{1 + \big(f'(x)\big)^2} \: \text{d}x \cdot \int_{0}^{2\pi}  \text{d}\theta \\[5pt]
&= \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \sqrt{1 + \big(f'(x)\big)^2} \: \text{d}x \cdot \big[ \theta \big]_{0}^{2\pi}  \\[5pt]
&= 2\pi \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\sqrt{1 + \big(f'(x)\big)^2 } \: \text{d}x.
\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "79f42de8-4cc4-576a-b367-c08bd87f8bcd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7638 :tutorial/title "Computing a Surface Area of Revolution"} :step/id #uuid "8c37f4ed-7df7-5a6c-855e-263d81b3f5b0" :step/math-academy-id 44313 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173085}} {:db/id 17592186173253 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $S$ is a surface parametrized by a differentiable vector-valued function

Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics.
